name: Tutor
seoDescription: Tutor insurance costs about $250/yr for solo General Liability. Covers in-home sessions, test-prep disputes, and abuse coverage for tutors working with minors.

industryContext.contextNote: Most tutors work alone, either online or in a student's home, a library, or their own home. Unlike most remote professions, tutors spend much of their time with minors, which brings supervision and abuse-allegation exposure that insurers take seriously. Parents are usually the paying client, so disputes over results or fees come from someone other than the student being taught.

riskFactors.title: Student Supervision Claims
riskFactors.description: Tutors working with minors carry supervision-related liability if a student is injured or a safety incident occurs during a session.

riskFactors.title: Educational Outcome Disputes
riskFactors.description: Parents or students who feel tutoring failed to deliver promised academic results can raise disputes over fees or service quality.

riskFactors.title: In-Home Session Liability
riskFactors.description: Tutors who travel to a student's home or host sessions in their own space face premises-related liability distinct from a school setting.

riskFactors.title: Abuse & Molestation Allegations
riskFactors.description: Any one-on-one work with minors carries the risk of an abuse allegation, and many General Liability policies exclude it unless a specific abuse and molestation endorsement is added.

claimScenarios.title: Student injured at the tutor's home
claimScenarios.scenario: A student trips on a loose rug on the way into a home tutoring session and fractures a wrist. The parents seek medical costs from the tutor, and the tutor's homeowners policy denies the claim because the injury happened during a business activity.
claimScenarios.coverage: General Liability. Homeowners policies commonly exclude injuries arising from business activities, even a small one run from home.

claimScenarios.title: Test-prep refund dispute
claimScenarios.scenario: A family pays for a 12-week SAT prep package marketed with a score increase. When the student's score doesn't improve, the parents claim the tutor misrepresented results and demand the fees back plus the cost of a replacement course.
claimScenarios.coverage: Professional liability (E&O) may cover defense costs for the negligence or misrepresentation claim. Refunds of your own fees are usually excluded, so avoid guaranteeing outcomes in marketing.

claimScenarios.title: Allegation after a one-on-one session
claimScenarios.scenario: A parent alleges inappropriate conduct during an unsupervised in-home session. Even when an allegation is unfounded, legal defense costs begin immediately.
claimScenarios.coverage: An abuse and molestation endorsement or standalone policy. Without it, many General Liability policies exclude these claims entirely, including defense costs.

faqs.question: Why do tutors need General Liability insurance?
faqs.answer: General Liability covers bodily injury or property damage that could occur during an in-person tutoring session, whether at the tutor's location or the student's home.

faqs.question: What is the average cost of business insurance for a tutor?
faqs.answer: A tutor in the $0-50k revenue tier pays an estimated $250 per year for baseline General Liability coverage, one of the lowest tiers modeled here.

faqs.question: Does a tutor working with children need special coverage?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ask specifically about abuse and molestation coverage, which many General Liability policies exclude by default. Some tutoring agencies, schools, and districts require it, along with a background check, before they will refer students to you.

faqs.question: Is online-only tutoring lower risk than in-person tutoring?
faqs.answer: Yes, online tutoring generally carries lower premises and supervision risk, though Professional Liability for educational outcome disputes still applies to both formats.

faqs.question: Does my homeowners or renters insurance cover tutoring at home?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Most homeowners and renters policies exclude liability arising from business activities, so a student injured during a paid session in your home may not be covered. Some insurers offer a home-business endorsement, but a General Liability policy is the more common solution for tutors who teach at home.

faqs.question: How much does a tutor pay for General Liability plus E&O?
faqs.answer: In this calculator, a solo tutor in the $0-50k revenue tier with one employee and GL + E&O is estimated at $366-$495 per year. A small tutoring business in the $150-500k tier with three staff is estimated at $485-$657, before any abuse and molestation endorsement, which the calculator doesn't price.

blogContent.whyThisRiskFactor: Tutors carry a 0.85 risk factor, one step above the 0.8 floor for fully remote document work. Physical risk is low but not zero: in-person sessions bring students into your home or you into theirs, and slip-and-fall injuries can happen in either. The bigger distinction is who you work with. Insurers price one-on-one work with minors carefully because supervision failures and abuse allegations, even unfounded ones, are expensive to defend. Online-only tutors remove most premises risk but keep the outcome-dispute exposure that comes with promising academic results to paying parents.
blogContent.howCalculated: The estimate multiplies the 0.85 factor by your revenue tier, then adds a per-employee cost for each tutor you employ, a fixed policy administration baseline, and a flat professional liability charge when GL + E&O is selected. Revenue matters because a larger tutoring business serves more students, and each added tutor is another adult working one-on-one with children. Abuse and molestation coverage isn't modeled, so if you work with minors, expect a real quote to add it as an endorsement.
blogContent.comparisonNote: Tutors price alongside mobile notaries, web designers, and photographers' assistants at 0.85. They sit below yoga instructors (1.15) and personal trainers (1.3), whose sessions involve physical exertion and a higher chance of bodily injury, and slightly above translators and copywriters (0.8), who rarely meet clients in person.
